findings.issue: The note dates Whitehouse's sighting of the Antiochene bishop to 'the 1860s'. Whitehouse's own text places it in 1853: the passage on Mar Kurillos Joyakin says he was 'also then living' a few miles off, in the account of the 1853 visit to Anyira. He records visiting the bishop's cottage, not seeing him 'at work'. A wrong date in a public note is a false claim.
findings.evidence: cic/texts/whitehouse_lingerings-of-light-in-a-dark-land_1873.txt 11286-11288 ('When at Anyira, in 1853, this Mar Kurillos was living...'), 11327-11345 (the 'then living' passage and the visit to his thatched cottage). The header gives Whitehouse as minister of the Government Church, Cochin.
findings.fix: Note: "In 1853 an English clergyman in Kerala, Thomas Whitehouse, met a bishop sent from Antioch. That bishop had been sent to check the reforming bishop Mar Athanasius. The reform party lived on as the Mar Thoma Church of the next century. The hill churches of the northeast lived on too, as Robert Frykenberg's history of Christianity in India shows." Also correct the drafter flag on the broke-with link that calls Whitehouse 'an outside witness in the 1860s'.

findings.issue: The note opens 'Baptist churches kept their old confession of faith in use after 1815.' The same page of McGlothlin that the note cites for the two English wings says the opposite for England: 'The old Confessions gradually fell into disuse, but no others took their places.' The confession that stayed in use was the Philadelphia Confession in America. The note also cites the 1813 printing as evidence for 'after 1815'. The link's type and grade can stand; the note overstates its own source.
findings.evidence: cic/texts/mcglothlin_baptist-confessions-of-faith_1911.txt 18757-18764 (English confessions 'fell into disuse'; the wings 'by degrees approached each other'), 19069-19092 (Charleston printings of 1813 and 1850, Sheppard's of 1831; 'still widely used, and in the South is probably the most influential').
findings.fix: Note: "In America many Baptist churches kept their old confession of faith in use through the century. W. J. McGlothlin, a Baptist historian, wrote in 1911 that new printings of the Philadelphia Confession came out in 1813, 1831 and 1850. In England the old confessions fell out of use, but he wrote that the two old wings of English Baptists slowly drew closer."

findings.issue: The note says Sandeen 'showed how this scheme was taught in American Bible schools. One was the school D. L. Moody opened in Chicago in 1886.' findings.issue: My call on the drafter's question: the General Council belongs to the American confessional revival, so the 1911 'return towards the confessional position' quote can carry Documented. But the note does not say which body Jacobs spoke for, and 'these old confessions' is not explained for a reader who does not know the Book of Concord. Its second sentence also rests on a passage about the colonial founding (the Mother Synod), not the nineteenth-century revival.
